summary: Kole Jain walks through web typography from the basics to a sizing formula. He covers font categories (serif, sans-serif, display, handwritten), the parts of a letter that matter to designers (baseline, x-height, cap height, letter spacing), and how many fonts to pair (one is entirely acceptable, two is the limit). He shows that font weight and text color (opacity) both control hierarchy, and argues that size should carry the heading, bold should make subheadings scannable, and paragraphs should stay at full opacity. For sizes he derives a type scale from the golden ratio (1.62), recommends its square root (1.27) for a full style guide and its cube root for dense or small-screen interfaces, then describes a fluid formula that scales each size between a 320 and a 1920 wide screen, optionally capped with min and max. Font colors, weights and pairings stay the same on every screen; only sizes change. For a design system this gives concrete defaults for font count, weight and opacity levels, the scale ratio, fluid sizing and line height.
key_ideas: Fonts fall into serif and sans-serif, plus two growing subgroups: display fonts for giant text and handwritten fonts that imitate handwriting.
Most everyday interfaces use sans-serif fonts because they read as cleaner and more modern.
Letter spacing should shrink proportionately as text grows and grow as text shrinks.
One font is entirely acceptable, two is the limit, three is pushing it and four invites problems.
Display and handwritten fonts must never be used for small paragraph text.
At small sizes, a thinner weight and a lighter color look alike because both reduce dark pixels, so either can set hierarchy.
Rank every text element first, then style it: size gives the heading attention, bold makes subheadings scannable, and paragraphs keep full opacity.
Making the smallest text also the lowest-contrast text hurts both usability and looks.
Eyeballing one page and building a style guide around it is not wrong, but a ratio-based type scale improves on it.
Multiplying by the golden ratio (1.62) at every step grows too fast; its square root (1.27) works across a whole style guide.
The cube root of the golden ratio gives a tighter scale for dashboards with many text styles or for mobile screens with less room.
Font colors, weights and pairings can stay constant on any screen; only font sizes change with screen size.
One fluid formula can scale each text size between the smallest and largest screen width without breakpoints.
Cap fluid sizes with min and max unless growing past the design widths works for the design.
Line height should rise as text gets smaller or lines get longer, and fall as text gets larger.
Always check text on the screens the design is intended for.

rules.rule: Use one or two font families; treat a third as a rare edge case and avoid four.
rules.why: One font is entirely acceptable and used by many industry-standard sites; three pushes the envelope and four invites problems.
rules.evidence: one font is entirely acceptable

rules.rule: If the system uses a single font, make it a sans-serif.
rules.why: A single-font site is generally sans-serif unless it deliberately wants an old-timey, medieval feel.
rules.evidence: if you opt for one it's generally going to be a sanser font

rules.rule: For a two-font pairing, pair a display font with a sans-serif, or a sans-serif with a serif; a handwritten font may replace the display font.
rules.why: These are the pairings seen on most modern websites.
rules.evidence: usually it's either a display font and a sansera font

rules.rule: Never set small paragraph text in a display font or a handwritten font; keep them for giant text elements.
rules.why: Their extra ornamentation and detail become impractical at paragraph size; the source calls it a design sin.
rules.evidence: that is 100% a design sin

rules.rule: Reduce letter spacing proportionately as text gets larger, and increase it as text gets smaller.
rules.why: Letter spacing is adjusted mostly by text size: larger text needs proportionately less space, smaller text more.
rules.evidence: larger text requiring proportionately less space and smaller text requiring proportionately more

rules.rule: Avoid ultra bold and ultra thin weights for regular text.
rules.why: Stay away from extremes when choosing weights for regular text.
rules.evidence: try and stay away from extremes with ultra bold and ultra thin

rules.rule: Set primary text at 100% opacity and secondary text somewhere between 40 and 70% opacity.
rules.why: Avoid extremes with font colors just as with weights; these two levels work for creating hierarchy.
rules.evidence: 100% opacity and somewhere between 40 to 70% is good

rules.rule: Make weight and color steps visually different enough that each level reads as a distinct level of hierarchy.
rules.why: Weights and colors only create hierarchy if the difference is visible.
rules.evidence: things are visually different enough to actually create hierarchy

rules.rule: Use either weight or color (opacity) to push small text forward or back; both work because each reduces the number of dark pixels.
rules.why: At small sizes a thinner weight and a lighter color look very similar.
rules.evidence: we can use both color and weights to manipulate hierarchy

rules.rule: Before styling, list every text element in order of importance (for example header first, subheadings second, paragraphs third), then apply font styles to match that order.
rules.why: You should literally be able to list the hierarchy of all text elements and style them accordingly.
rules.evidence: you should literally be able to list the hierarchy of all the text elements

rules.rule: Do not make paragraph text lighter than the rest; keep paragraphs at 100% opacity so the smallest text is not also the lowest-contrast text.
rules.why: Smallest text with the least contrast is neither very usable nor aesthetic.
rules.evidence: we want the opacity to be 100%

rules.rule: Let a large size carry the heading's emphasis instead of automatically also making it bold and full-strength.
rules.why: Making the heading large already gives it the most attention regardless of thickness or opacity.
rules.evidence: the header doesn't automatically become bolded

rules.rule: Make subheadings bold so they are easy to scan and stand out more than paragraph text.
rules.why: Subheadings should be easily scannable and pop more than the paragraph.
rules.evidence: we'll make it bold

rules.rule: Derive font sizes from a scale ratio instead of eyeballing one page and building the style guide around it.
rules.why: Eyeballing one page is not wrong but can be improved with a ratio-based scale.
rules.evidence: it's not wrong but it can be improved

rules.rule: With only a heading and body text, make the heading the body size multiplied by 1.62.
rules.why: Multiplying body text by the golden ratio gives a heading size that looks pretty good in the most basic layouts.
rules.evidence: multiply the body text by 1.62 to get the size of the header text

rules.rule: Do not multiply every step of a multi-size scale by the full golden ratio (1.62) from a 16 px base.
rules.why: Sizes grow too large too quickly: with four header sizes and a paragraph the largest header reaches 110 pixels.
rules.evidence: our font sizes start to get very large a little too quickly

rules.rule: Use the square root of the golden ratio, 1.27, as the ratio between consecutive font sizes in a full style guide.
rules.why: It leaves room for an in-between size such as a subheading and works across many font sizes.
rules.evidence: square rooted it to get 1.27

rules.rule: Use the cube root of the golden ratio for a tighter scale when the interface has many font styles (such as a dashboard) or little room (such as mobile).
rules.why: It gives smaller scaling steps when you need them.
rules.evidence: Cube rooting the golden ratio

rules.rule: Scale each font size fluidly: smallest size + (largest size - smallest size) x (current screen width - smallest width) / (largest width - smallest width), instead of setting sizes at breakpoints.
rules.why: Adjusting each size at breakpoints could be messy; one line of CSS scales text for every screen size.
rules.evidence: with this single line of CSS we can have scale text

rules.rule: Use 320 as the smallest and 1920 as the largest screen width in the fluid formula, adjusting if needed.
rules.why: These are the widths the source generally uses, while noting you can play with them.
rules.evidence: I generally use 1920 as the largest width and 320 as the smallest width

rules.rule: Cap fluid font sizes: wrap the formula in max() with the lower bound and min() with the upper bound, unless letting text keep growing on larger screens works for the design.
rules.why: The linear formula keeps producing larger or smaller sizes past the chosen widths.
rules.evidence: set a cap on the size with a simple Min and Max

rules.rule: Increase line height as text gets smaller or lines get longer, and reduce it as text gets larger.
rules.why: It makes text easier to read.
rules.evidence: the line height should increase to make things easier to read

rules.rule: Set paragraph line height around 150% and heading line height around 110 to 130%.
rules.why: A rule of thumb for readable text; automatic line height falls off toward extremely large text.
rules.evidence: for paragraph text line height should be around 150 %

rules.rule: Do not leave line height on auto for very large text.
rules.why: Most designers leave line height on auto, but it falls off a little for extremely large text.
rules.evidence: especially towards extremely large text it falls off

rules.rule: Review designs on the screen sizes they were intended for to check text size, colors and fonts.
rules.why: It is the way to see whether the typography actually makes sense.
rules.evidence: view your designs on the screen they were intended for

rules.rule: Keep font pairings, weights and colors the same on every screen size; let only font sizes change with the screen.
rules.why: Colors, weights and pairings can stay constant on any screen, while sizes change with screen size.
rules.evidence: font colors weights and pairings can stay constant on any screen

rules.rule: If a third font is used, pair a display font and a sans-serif with a third font reserved for small details or captions under images.
rules.why: That is the three-font pattern the source has seen elsewhere and uses on his own portfolio, framed as an edge case.
rules.evidence: a s font for small details or captions under images

decisions.question: How many fonts should the system use, and how should they be paired?

options.name: One font (usually sans-serif)
options.effect: Clean and consistent; hierarchy comes from size, weight and color.
options.when: Default; many industry-standard sites do this.

options.name: Two fonts: display + sans-serif
options.effect: Headlines get personality from an ornamented display font while body text stays clean.
options.when: Most modern websites that want expressive headings.

options.name: Two fonts: sans-serif + serif
options.effect: Mixes a modern sans with a more traditional, authoritative serif.
options.when: When some text should read as more classic or editorial [inferred].

options.name: Two fonts: handwritten + sans-serif
options.effect: A handwritten font takes the display role for a personal, human feel.
options.when: Acceptable in place of a display font.

options.name: Three fonts: display + sans-serif + small-detail font
options.effect: A third font (Courier Prime on Kole's portfolio) marks small details or image captions.
options.when: Edge case; pushing the envelope.

decisions.recommendation: One font is entirely acceptable and two is the limit; three is pushing it and four is asking for problems.

decisions.question: Which font category should the main text use?

options.name: Sans-serif
options.effect: Cleaner and more modern; what most everyday interfaces use (YouTube, Instagram, X).

options.name: Serif
options.effect: Reads as older and perhaps more authoritative; said to be easier to read at small sizes.
options.when: Books, magazines, or an old-timey, medieval style site.

options.name: Display
options.effect: Extra ornamentation and detail for giant text.
options.when: Only for large headline elements, never paragraphs.

options.name: Handwritten

options.when: As a display font substitute, never for small paragraph text.

decisions.recommendation: Use a sans-serif when there is only one font; keep display and handwritten fonts for large text.

decisions.question: Should hierarchy between text levels come from weight, color, or both?

options.name: Color (opacity) only
options.effect: Same weight throughout; lower levels are lighter (for example 40 to 70% opacity against 100%).
options.when: When a single weight should be kept; shown in a layout that only uses color.

options.name: Weight only
options.effect: Same color throughout; levels differ by thickness.
options.when: When all text should stay at full opacity; shown in a layout that only uses weights.

options.name: Both
options.effect: Weight and color changes used together across levels.
options.when: The source says both can manipulate hierarchy but does not show a combined layout.

decisions.recommendation: Both work because at small sizes thinner weight and lighter color look similar; avoid extremes (ultra bold, ultra thin) and make each level visibly different.
decisions.evidence: in this layout I'm only using color and here I'm only using weights

decisions.question: How should a heading, subheadings and paragraphs be styled to show their order?

options.name: Bold full-opacity heading, plain subheadings, lighter paragraphs
options.effect: The predictable approach; the smallest text ends up with the least contrast.
options.when: Not recommended: neither very usable nor aesthetic.

options.name: Large plain heading, bold subheadings, full-opacity paragraphs
options.effect: Size alone makes the heading lead, subheadings are easy to scan, and body text stays readable.
options.when: Recommended starting point.

decisions.recommendation: Let size carry the heading, bold the subheadings for scanning, and keep paragraphs at 100% opacity.

options.when: Only a heading and body text.

options.name: Square root of the golden ratio, 1.27
options.effect: Gentler steps that leave room for in-between sizes like subheadings; looks subtly better applied to a design.
options.when: A full style guide with several sizes.

options.name: Cube root of the golden ratio
options.effect: Even smaller steps between sizes.
options.when: Dashboards with many font styles, or mobile interfaces with less room.

options.name: Eyeball one page
options.effect: Sizes set by feel on one page, then a style guide built around it.
options.when: The source's old method: not wrong, but can be improved.

decisions.recommendation: Use the square root of the golden ratio (1.27) from a 16 px base for a full style guide; use the cube root for dense or small-screen interfaces.
decisions.evidence: what if we took the golden ratio square rooted it

decisions.question: Should text sizes change with screen width, and how?

options.name: Breakpoints
options.effect: Each text size is adjusted at set screen widths; could be messy when close control over sizes is needed.
options.when: The previous common approach.

options.name: Fluid formula
options.effect: Each size scales linearly from its smallest value at a 320 wide screen to its largest at a 1920 wide screen, with no breakpoints.
options.when: When text should look right on every screen size.

decisions.recommendation: Use the single-line fluid formula so text scales from mobile to desktop without breakpoints.
decisions.evidence: without the need for any break points

decisions.question: Should fluid text keep growing or shrinking beyond the chosen smallest and largest screen widths?

options.name: Uncapped
options.effect: Larger screens than the largest width get even larger text; smaller screens get smaller text.
options.when: If that works in the design.

options.name: Capped with min and max
options.effect: Text stops at the lower and upper bounds regardless of screen size.
options.when: Otherwise.

decisions.recommendation: Cap it unless growth works for the design: max() holds the lower bound and min() holds the upper bound.
decisions.evidence: if that works in the design fantastic otherwise you can set a cap

decisions.question: How should line height be set?

options.name: Auto
options.effect: What most designers use about 95% of the time; falls off a little toward extremely large text.
options.when: The common habit the source moves away from.

options.name: Percentage by role
options.effect: Around 150% for paragraphs and 110 to 130% for headings; higher for smaller text or longer lines, lower for larger text.
options.when: The source's rule of thumb.

decisions.recommendation: Set line height explicitly: around 150% for paragraph text and 110 to 130% for heading text.

process.detail: Start with one sans-serif font; add a second (display, serif or handwritten) only if needed. Keep display and handwritten fonts away from paragraph text.
List every text element in order of importance, for example header first, subheadings second, paragraphs third.
Start from a 16 px base and multiply by the square root of the golden ratio (1.27) for each step; use the cube root for dashboards or mobile, or 1.62 when there is only a heading and body text.
Avoid ultra bold and ultra thin. Use 100% opacity and a second level between 40 and 70%. Let size carry the heading, bold the subheadings and keep paragraphs at 100% opacity.
Tighten proportionately for large text and loosen for small text.
For each style, pick its size on the smallest screen (320 wide) and the largest (1920 wide), then compute smallest size + (largest size - smallest size) x (current width - 320) / (1920 - 320).
Unless growth past those widths suits the design, wrap the formula in max() with the lower bound and min() with the upper bound.
About 150% for paragraphs and 110 to 130% for headings; raise it for smaller text or longer lines, lower it for larger text.
View the design on the screens it is intended for to confirm sizes, colors and fonts make sense.

caveats: Opinion framed as 'mathematically perfect': the golden-ratio scale and fluid formula are the creator's personal method ('my magic equation'), not a standard.
The actual CSS line is described in words, not shown in the transcript; the transcript does not name clamp() or viewport units.
The cube-root value of the golden ratio is recommended but never stated as a number (about 1.17 [inferred]).
Historical and readability claims about serif fonts (ancient Greek origin, easier to read small) are stated without evidence.
The Comic Sans remark is a joke, not guidance.
